prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks: the magic-wavelength lattice, which allows many neutral atoms to be interrogated without a trapping-light shift, and its development to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability, enabling laboratory tests of gravitational redshift and of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye, and after round 1 I hold the position more firmly than before. The scientific content is a new regime, not a refinement. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the trapping-light shift, so a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be held and interrogated at once without perturbing the clock transition. That is a different physical mechanism from the frequency comb (a ruler for optical frequencies) and from the control of single trapped ions (one quantum system at a time). The many-atom regime is what made the statistics, and with it the 10^-18 systematic uncertainty, the millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, the many-body clock physics and the constant-variation and dark-matter searches possible. Robustness is the other test I apply: JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE have reproduced and surpassed each other across Sr, Yb and Hg for over a decade, and optical clocks of different types agree with each other. To answer the chair's question for the committee, my one-sentence difference from 2005 and 2012 is that those prizes honoured the tool for counting optical cycles and the control of a single quantum system, whereas this one honours the scheme that lets a macroscopic ensemble of atoms act as a clock without distorting the transition, and the new measurements that follow. On the citation, it should rest only on demonstrated performance and demonstrated physics, and say nothing about a redefinition of the second. I would also not add a second part just to fill the prize. None of the candidates the chair lists is clearly ready with a credit set that survives scrutiny, and I do not think a weak second part improves a strong first one.
statement.case_against: The honest objections remain three. First, lineage: Ye shared the 2005 prize and the field has a long record of clock-related prizes, so some readers will see an evolution of earlier recognition. I think the many-atom magic-wavelength regime answers this but I cannot claim it settles the question for Mehlig. Second, priority: the magic-wavelength idea was developed in near-parallel by several groups, and Lemonde, Takamoto and the Sr and Yb community are not credited. I am a superconducting-circuit theorist and have not checked the early-2000s chronology against the original papers, so I rely on Lindroth and Kroll for it. If that check showed that the proposal, or the first demonstration, clearly belongs to someone outside Katori and Ye, I would change my position. Third, a clock is an instrument, and the committee has to be comfortable that the discovery being recognised is a new physical regime opened by measurement, not the instrument alone. I believe it is, but this is a judgement and the citation has to make that case explicitly.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the prize should go to the original experiment (Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice clock) rather than to the later and more accurate realisation by Ye, and wants the priority record reviewed before accepting the pair without qualification.
responses.response: I think this is the right criterion and I read the record as supporting the pair rather than a single name. Katori's proposal and first demonstration made the lattice clock exist. The step that turned it into a regime of physics, with systematic uncertainty near 10^-18, many-atom effects and the redshift measurement across millimetres, was largely done in Ye's laboratory, and the two programmes are linked in the literature that followed. That is two distinct decisive contributions to one achievement, not a later group improving someone else's result. I would still like the chronology of the early-2000s proposals confirmed by Lindroth or Kroll, and I would accept a citation wording that names the lattice scheme and the 10^-18 realisation separately so that each contribution is visible.

responses.point: Mehlig, who keeps KPZ (B056) first and ranked B002 low, regards clocks as precision technology that overlaps with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and asks for a case that this is a discovery about nature.
responses.response: I take the disagreement as one of weight and I do not think it can be settled by counting. What I can offer is a concrete test: lattice clocks have made physics measurements that were not possible before, namely resolving the gravitational redshift over a millimetre, limiting the drift of fundamental constants, and constraining dark-matter couplings, and they have exposed many-body shifts in the clock that nobody had to consider with a single ion. That is nature answering a question, not only a device getting better. I also share your instinct about KPZ's conceptual clarity, and I agree that the experiment is clean. My difficulty is the one you state yourself, that Parisi and the exact-solution authors are outside Kardar, Zhang and Takeuchi, and Kroll and Lindroth question how far the confirmation extends beyond one liquid-crystal system. For me that makes B056 not yet a sound three-name prize, but I respect that it is a serious statistical-physics case.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps topological insulators (B015) first as a verified discovery of a new state of matter, argues the fairness problem affects the choice of names and not the existence of the discovery, and distinguishes the lineage with the 2016 prize from my circuit QED case.
responses.response: I accept your distinction and it is the reason I no longer defend B017: the same Josephson-circuit platform was honoured last year and I am too close to it to be an objective judge. On B015 I am a guest in condensed matter and defer to you on the physics, which I find convincing as a confirmed discovery. My remaining hesitation is the one you list. The Kane-Mele graphene mechanism is not what was observed, the HgTe proposal that made Molenkamp's experiment possible came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and Fu, Moore, Hasan and Cava are outside the trio. Unless the committee finds a defensible three-name credit I cannot prefer it, but I have moved it up as an alternative because your case that it is a discovery, not an instrument, deserves a real hearing if the clock credit fails the priority check.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B002 first, says the committee must argue in the citation that the content is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and flags that Ye already shares the 2005 recognition.
responses.response: I agree and I have written the citation in that spirit, with the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-atom 10^-18 regime named as the new content. On Ye's earlier prize, I do not think it should count against him: the 2005 work was on the comb, and the achievement here is different and independently decisive. As the atomic physicist you are best placed to check whether Pottier, Lemonde or others anticipated the magic-wavelength proposal and whether that changes the credit. Since I stated in round 1 that I would not oppose waiting if something clearer were imminent, I should be clear that I no longer think waiting is needed: the redshift, the cross-laboratory agreement and the fundamental-physics tests are all in hand without a redefinition of the second.

uncertainties: Early-2000s priority of the magic-wavelength idea (Katori versus Pottier, Lemonde and others) has not been checked against original papers by anyone in the committee yet, and could change the credited pair.
Whether the committee accepts that the many-atom lattice regime is a distinct discovery from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which Mehlig does not.
Whether the Sr and Yb community around Lemonde and Takamoto is adequately handled by a two-person credit.
Whether I am too favourable to a metrology candidate and too unfavourable to condensed-matter discoveries such as B015 and B038, where I defer to colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits, so B017 (circuit QED) and B052 (Cleland's phonon-qubit work) are close to my own research community. I will recuse myself from any decision on B017 and flag B052 if it becomes decisive. Neither is part of my preferred configuration. I have no specific tie to B002 candidates Katori or Ye. My alternatives B033 and B015 are outside my field and not connected to my own work. No other specific conflict is apparent from my profile.
